post_text:
I assumed separating reads from writes with CQRS would instantly cure our database lock contention.

I split our monolithic transaction service into two clean JVM deployments, routing queries to a read-replica and commands to the primary database.

The deployment went flawlessly, and our primary database CPU dropped to near zero. I felt an immediate rush of triumph as the dashboards glowed green, but a hollow feeling quickly replaced it.

The silence was deceptive.

The read-replica began lagging by minutes under the heavy write load. Users saw stale balances, panicked, and initiated duplicate withdrawals that our read-model allowed because it did not know the funds were already gone.

We lost thousands of dollars in minutes before we could roll back the deployment.

What I learned:

Eventual consistency is not just a technical trade-off; it is a business risk that will break your system if your domain cannot tolerate stale data.
lesson_extracted: Eventual consistency is a business risk, not just a technical trade-off, and it will fail if your domain cannot tolerate stale data.
